topicos.aulaTitulo: First Steps in German
topicos.titulo: The four patterns that unlock dozens of words
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German «ei» sounds /aɪ/, like eye: «Wein» and «Eis». STEP 2: German «ie» usually represents long /iː/, as in English see: «Bier» and «Brief». STEP 3: German «eu» and «äu» are pronounced /ɔʏ/, roughly like oy in boy: «Euro» and «Häuser». STEP 4: German «au» sounds /aʊ/, like ow in cow: «Haus» and «Auto». Now compare «Wein» and «Wien»: the spelling difference changes both sound and meaning. The patterns are reliable guides for these common words, not a promise that every letter group has only one pronunciation in every context.
topicos.comparacao: English speakers may see ei and say 'ee' or 'ay'. In German, start by trusting ei = eye and ie = ee. Train both directions: see the spelling and predict the sound; hear the sound and choose the spelling.

erros.motivo: Wien has ie /iː/; it means Vienna.

topicos.aulaTitulo: First Steps in German
topicos.titulo: Consonant clusters you can read on sight
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «sch» sounds /ʃ/ as in English ship: «Schule», «Fisch». STEP 2: «sp» and «st» at the beginning of a native German word or stressed stem normally start with /ʃp/ and /ʃt/: «Sport», «Stein». STEP 3: The two main sounds of «ch» are [ç] after front vowels (as in «ich») and [x] after back vowels (as in «Buch»). English has no exact everyday equivalent to [ç]; Scottish loch is a useful approximation for [x]. STEP 4: «tsch» sounds /tʃ/ as in English church: «Deutsch». STEP 5: «pf», «qu», «ck» and «ng» have their own patterns: «Apfel», «Quelle», «Jacke», «singen». Listen before trying to imitate unfamiliar sounds.
topicos.comparacao: English 'ch' in church is /tʃ/. German «ch» is usually [ç] or [x]; German «tsch» gives you the English church sound. Do not pronounce «ich» as English 'itch'.

erros.motivo: Initial sp in this German word is /ʃp/.

topicos.aulaTitulo: First Steps in German
topicos.titulo: Choose the greeting and the register
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: For a friend, use «Hallo!» and «Wie geht’s?»; answer «Gut, danke! Und dir?». STEP 2: For a stranger or a formal setting, «Guten Tag!» and «Wie geht es Ihnen?» are useful polite options; you can ask back «Und Ihnen?». STEP 3: «Guten Morgen» is a morning greeting, «Guten Tag» a daytime greeting and «Guten Abend» an evening greeting. STEP 4: «Gute Nacht» is normally said when someone is going to bed, not as an evening arrival greeting. STEP 5: «Tschüs!» is an informal goodbye; «Auf Wiedersehen!» is a more formal farewell. German choices depend on the context, not simply the clock.
topicos.comparacao: English 'you' does not distinguish du and Sie. German does: «dir» with a friend, «Ihnen» in polite speech. Learn the right phrase for the situation before studying the grammar behind the pronoun endings.

tabela.german: Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen?

erros.motivo: Use the evening greeting when arriving; good night is associated with going to sleep.
The polite form is Ihnen, not dir.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.titulo: Word order and the first questions
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: listen to «Ich heiße Lea.» and then «Wie heißt du?». To say your name, the verb is «heißen», which means to be called. STEP 2: in German, the conjugated verb always stays in the SECOND position of the sentence. In «Ich heiße Lea», the «ich» takes the first position, and «heiße» takes the second. STEP 3: in questions with a question word, that word takes the first place. Examples: «wie», which means how and reads «vee», and «woher», which means where from and reads «voh-HAIR». The verb stays second: «Wie heißt du?» and «Woher kommst du?». STEP 4: in a yes/no question, the verb goes to the front: «Heißt du Lea?». German needs no «do» here. Answer «Ja» or «Nein». STEP 5: the verb changes its ending according to the person. With «ich», it ends in «e»: «ich heiße», «ich komme». With «du», it ends in «st»: «du kommst». In «heißen», the «ß» already makes an «s» sound, so you add only the «t»: «du heißt». STEP 6: do not forget the pronoun. German, like English, needs it: «Ich komme aus Brasilien», never just «Komme aus Brasilien». STEP 7: a warning. In the words «der Name» and «der Vorname», the «der» is an article. You learn articles in lesson 3. For now, repeat the «der» together with the word.
topicos.comparacao: In English the verb also comes right after the subject, and you cannot drop the «I» either. The difference is that German fixes the verb in the second position even when another word opens the sentence, so the subject can end up after the verb (like «Today come I»).

linhas.question: Wie heißt du?
linhas.en: What is your name? My name is Anna.

linhas.question: Wie heißen Sie?
linhas.en: What is your name (formal)? My name is Müller.

linhas.question: Woher kommst du?
linhas.en: Where are you from? I am from Brazil.

linhas.question: Woher kommen Sie?
linhas.en: Where are you from (formal)? I am from Brazil.

erros.motivo: The conjugated verb stays in the second position, right after the «ich».
In a question with «wie», the verb comes right after the question word.
The pronoun «ich» cannot be dropped; German needs it, just as English needs «I».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.titulo: Sein: to be
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «sein» is the German verb for «to be», and it reads «zine». STEP 2: «sein» is irregular and changes a lot, like English «am / are / is». Listen to the forms: «ich bin», «du bist», «er, sie, es ist», «wir sind», «ihr seid», «sie sind». Watch out: «sind» reads «zint» and «seid» reads «zite». STEP 3: use «sein» to say who you are: «Ich bin Brasilianer» or «Das ist Lea». STEP 4: use it also to say how you are or where you are: «Ich bin müde» and «Wir sind hier». Just like English «to be», one verb does all of these jobs. STEP 5: to make a negative, put «nicht» after the verb: «Ich bin nicht müde». STEP 6: in a yes/no question, the verb goes to the front: «Bist du müde?». Answer: «Ja, ich bin müde.» or «Nein, ich bin nicht müde.»
topicos.comparacao: English has one verb for this, «to be», and German has one too: «sein». The catch is that each person has its own very different form, and you have to memorise them, just as you do with «am / are / is» in English, only with more forms.

erros.motivo: Each person has its own form. With «ich», the form is always «bin».
With «wir», the form is «sind». The form «ist» belongs to «er», «sie» and «es».
The verb stays in the second position, and the «nicht» comes after it.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.titulo: You, you all, you (formal): du, ihr e Sie
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to talk to ONE person you are close to, such as a friend, family member, child or young colleague, use «du». STEP 2: to talk to SEVERAL people you are close to, use «ihr» (like «you all» or «you guys»). STEP 3: to talk to someone you do not know well, or to show respect, use «Sie», which reads «zee». It works for sir, madam or ladies and gentlemen, one person or several. In writing, formal «Sie» always starts with a capital S. STEP 4: with «Sie» the verb has the same form as for «they»: «Sie sind» and «Wie heißen Sie?». STEP 5: when in doubt, use «Sie». The other person will offer you the «du» when they want to.
topicos.comparacao: English has just one «you» for everyone. In German, the choice between «du» and «Sie» is compulsory, and it changes the verb in the whole sentence.

erros.motivo: With «Sie» the verb stays in the plural, even for one single person.
With «du», the form of «sein» is «bist». «Sind» belongs to «wir» and «sie».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.titulo: Nacionalidades e idiomas
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say where you are from, use «Ich komme aus» and the country: «Ich komme aus Brasilien». STEP 2: most countries take no article: «Brasilien», «Deutschland», «Portugal». Switzerland is an exception, and has the article «die»: «die Schweiz». For now, memorise the ready-made sentence: «Ich komme aus der Schweiz». You will understand why later on. STEP 3: to say the nationality of a man, use «Brasilianer». For a woman, add «in»: «Brasilianerin». STEP 4: after «sein», the nationality comes without an article, as in English: «Ich bin Brasilianer», I am Brazilian. STEP 5: languages take no article either, and are written with a capital letter: «Ich spreche Deutsch». STEP 6: the verb «sprechen», which means to speak, is irregular with «du» and «er»: «ich spreche», «du sprichst», «er spricht». The «sp» at the start sounds like «shp», as you saw in lesson 1.
topicos.comparacao: In English one word often does double duty: «Portuguese» is a language and also what a person from Portugal is, and «German» is both the language and a nationality. In German these are separate words: the country, «Brasilien», the person, «Brasilianer», and the language, «Portugiesisch».

exemplos.ru: Ich komme aus Brasilien. Ich bin Brasilianer.
exemplos.pt: I am from Brazil. I am Brazilian.

exemplos.ru: Sie kommt aus Deutschland. Sie ist Deutsche.
exemplos.pt: She is from Germany. She is German.

erros.motivo: For nationality, the natural way is to say it without an article, as in English.
For a woman, the word gets the ending «in».
The language has its own form, with no ending: «Deutsch».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: English has no grammatical gender: it only has «the». German has three genders: der (masculine), die (feminine) and das (neuter). In the plural, the article is always die. STEP 2: never learn Tisch. Learn der Tisch.
topicos.comparacao: German gender does not follow logic, and English gives you no clue, because it has only «the». Do not assume «der» just because a thing sounds masculine. The gender is part of the word and must be learned together with it.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: Der, die, das: the three genders
topicos.explicacao: In German every noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). The gender does not follow logic: «das Mädchen» (the girl) is neuter. So always memorise the article together with the word. EVERY noun is written with a CAPITAL letter, anywhere in the sentence. There are clues in the endings, with exceptions: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion, -ie and most words in -e are feminine; -er, -ling and -ismus are masculine; -chen, -lein, -um and -ment are neuter. Days of the week, months and seasons are masculine.
topicos.comparacao: In English we say «he» or «she» for people and «it» for things, but German gender is a property of the word itself, and it often does not match what you would expect: «das Kind» (the child) is neuter.

linhas.example: der Mann, der Tisch, der Vater
die Frau, die Lampe, die Mutter
das Kind, das Buch, das Haus
die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Nation, die Familie, die Lampe
das Mädchen, das Museum, das Dokument
der Montag, der Juli, der Sommer

erros.motivo: Kind is neuter and the noun takes a capital letter.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the endings of the words in each group. STEP 2: Group A: die Zeitung, die Wohnung, die Gesundheit, die Möglichkeit, die Freundschaft, die Information. STEP 3: Group B: das Mädchen, das Brötchen, das Büchlein, das Instrument. STEP 4: Group C: der Lehrer, der Computer, der Frühling, der Montag, der Dezember. STEP 5: Which endings mark group A and group B? What do the words in group C have in common, besides the ending? STEP 6: Now look at the plurals:

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: The plural: five patterns
topicos.explicacao: The German plural is formed in five ways: -e (der Tisch → die Tische), -(e)n (die Lampe → die Lampen), -er (das Buch → die Bücher), no ending (der Lehrer → die Lehrer) and -s (das Auto → die Autos, common in foreign words). Many words also take an umlaut on the vowel (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü), a bit like English «foot → feet» or «mouse → mice». There is no safe rule: learn the plural together with the noun. The definite article of the plural is always «die», for all three genders.
topicos.comparacao: The English plural is almost always just «-s» (apart from a few oddities like «children»). The German plural has five forms, and you have to memorise them with each word.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: Ein, eine, kein: the indefinite article and the negative
topicos.explicacao: «Ein» and «eine» are «a / an»: ein Mann, eine Frau, ein Kind. In the plural there is no indefinite article: «Das sind Bücher». To negate a noun, use «kein» (or «keine»), which has the same endings as «ein»: «Das ist kein Tisch» (this is not a table). For «this is» use «das ist» in the singular and «das sind» in the plural.

erros.motivo: In the plural there is no indefinite article.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is guessing the gender (die Haus for “the house”, der Sonne for “the sun”) or putting an article before a profession after sein, as English does (Ich bin eine Lehrerin; English says “I am a teacher”). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: count the positions. One block, then the verb. Always in that order.
topicos.comparacao: In English the subject stays right in front of the verb, even after a time word: “Today I live in Munich.” The same order in German gives Heute ich wohne in München, which is wrong. In German, the verb never leaves the second position. When something other than the subject opens the sentence, the subject goes after the verb.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.titulo: The regular present tense: stem + ending
topicos.explicacao: Almost all German verbs end in -en in the infinitive. Remove the -en to find the stem and add the endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. If the stem ends in -t or -d (arbeiten, finden), an -e- is inserted before -st and before -t, to make pronunciation easier: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. If the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z (heißen, reisen), the «du» loses the -s of the ending: du heißt, du reist. The forms «wir», «sie» and «Sie» are the same as the infinitive.
topicos.comparacao: In English the verb hardly changes («I speak, you speak, we speak») except for the «-s» of «he / she / it speaks». German has more endings than that, but only five different ones, and «wir», «sie» and «Sie» repeat the infinitive.

erros.motivo: Stem in -t: an -e- is inserted before the -st.
Stem in -s: the «du» loses the -s of the ending.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Read the four sentences and notice where the verb and the subject are. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: Which word does not change place in any of the four? STEP 4: What happens to Tom when something else opens the sentence? STEP 5: In sentence 4, how many words come before the verb?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.titulo: The verb in second position, questions and negation
topicos.explicacao: The conjugated verb always stays in 2nd position. If the sentence begins with another element (today, tomorrow), the subject goes after the verb: «Heute arbeite ich.» In yes/no questions, the verb comes in 1st place: «Wohnst du in Berlin?» In questions with a question word, the word comes first and the verb second: «Wo wohnst du?» The negation «nicht» goes after the verb («Ich arbeite nicht») or before what is being negated («Ich wohne nicht in Berlin»). To say that you like doing something, use «gern» after the verb: «Ich lerne gern Deutsch».

erros.motivo: The conjugated verb stays in 2nd position.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is leaving the subject stuck at the front after an adverb of time or place: Heute ich lerne. It seems natural because English does it that way, but in German the verb is a fixed magnet in Position 2 and the subject goes after it (inversion). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Like English, German uses no article before the possessive. “My father” is mein Vater, never der mein Vater. STEP 2: the owner chooses the stem. The thing owned chooses the ending.
topicos.comparacao: English «his» and «her» agree only with the owner: it is the owner that decides. German possessives agree with two things: the owner (sein = his, ihr = her) and the thing owned, which decides the ending.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.titulo: Haben and the direct object
topicos.explicacao: «Haben» (to have) is irregular. The direct object of «haben» goes into the accusative. In the masculine singular, «ein» becomes «einen» and «kein» becomes «keinen»; in the feminine, the neuter and the plural nothing changes: «Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe eine Schwester. Ich habe ein Kind. Ich habe keine Kinder».
topicos.comparacao: In English the direct object does not change form (apart from pronouns: «he» becomes «him»). In German the masculine changes: «ein Bruder» (who someone is) becomes «einen Bruder» (what someone has).

tabelas.title: The accusative changes only the masculine

erros.motivo: To negate a noun use kein/keine.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the endings of mein. STEP 2: Now look at the owner. STEP 3: Tom und seine Mutter. Lena und ihr Vater. STEP 4: Camila und ihr Bruder. STEP 5: Questions: STEP 6: The endings of mein remind you of which words you already know? STEP 7: What decides between sein and ihr? STEP 8: What decides between seine and sein?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.titulo: Mein, dein, sein...: the possessives
topicos.explicacao: The ending of a possessive agrees with the thing OWNED (gender and number), not with the owner; the owner only chooses the stem (mein, dein, sein, ihr...): «mein Vater», «meine Mutter», «mein Kind», «meine Eltern». The endings are those of «ein»: no ending in the masculine and the neuter, -e in the feminine and the plural. «Sein» means «his» and «ihr» means «her» (and also «their»); «Ihr», with a capital letter, is the formal «your». Careful: «unser» and «euer» lose the -e- before the ending: unsere, eure.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.titulo: Numbers from 11 to 20 and age
topicos.explicacao: From 13 to 19 the numbers are formed with the base + «-zehn» (like English «-teen»): dreizehn, vierzehn, fünfzehn... Careful: 16 = sechzehn (loses the -s) and 17 = siebzehn (loses the -en). 11 (elf) and 12 (zwölf) are special; 20 is zwanzig. To say your age: «Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt» or just «Ich bin zwanzig». Question: «Wie alt bist du?».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is mixing up the owner and the thing owned (Lena und sein Vater instead of ihr Vater) or putting an article before the possessive (der mein Bruder; English never says “the my brother”, and German does not allow it either). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: halb looks ahead to the hour that is coming. Halb vier is half an hour before four, so 3:30.
topicos.comparacao: Four stumbling blocks await English speakers.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: Numbers from 21 to 100
topicos.explicacao: From 21 to 99 German reads the unit first and then the tens, joined by «und»: 25 = fünfundzwanzig («five and twenty»). «Eins» becomes «ein»: 21 = einundzwanzig. Be careful with 16 and 60 (sechzehn, sechzig) and with 17 and 70 (siebzehn, siebzig): they lose letters. 30 is dreißig, with ß. The hundreds add up: zweihundert (200), 101 = hunderteins. A thousand is «tausend». Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit.
topicos.comparacao: English says «twenty-five» (the tens come first). German says «five and twenty», like old-fashioned English.

erros.motivo: The unit comes first, joined by «und».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the numbers. STEP 2: Look at the times. STEP 3: Look at the dates.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: Telling the time
topicos.explicacao: Questions: «Wie spät ist es?» or «Wie viel Uhr ist es?». Answer: «Es ist acht Uhr.» For the time something happens: «Um wie viel Uhr?» — «Um acht Uhr.» In everyday speech: «fünf nach acht» (8:05), «Viertel nach acht» (8:15), «halb neun» (8:30), «Viertel vor neun» (8:45), «fünf vor neun» (8:55). Careful: «halb neun» is HALF AN HOUR BEFORE nine, that is, 8:30. In official use (trains, TV) the 24-hour clock is used: «acht Uhr dreißig», «vierzehn Uhr fünfzehn».
topicos.comparacao: In English «half past eight» looks back to the hour that has passed. In German «halb neun» looks ahead to the hour that is coming, the nine.

erros.motivo: «halb drei» is half an hour before three.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: Dias da semana, meses e a data
topicos.explicacao: The days of the week and the months are all masculine (der Montag, der Januar). «Am» + day = on (Monday): «am Montag». «Im» + month = in (January): «im Mai». The date uses the ordinal with a dot: «der 5. Oktober» (der fünfte Oktober). Up to 19, the ordinal is the number + -te (der vierte); 1, 3, 7 and 8 are special (erste, dritte, siebte, achte). From 20 on, the number + -ste (der zwanzigste). In «am 5. Oktober», you read «am fünften Oktober».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is reading halb drei as 3:30, like English «half past three» (and arriving an hour late!), and mixing up the prepositions of time (um for hours, am for days and dates, im for months and seasons). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German marks the function in the article. But only in the masculine. That gives two traps: STEP 2: only the masculine changes. So only ask whether the word is der. If it is not, nothing happens.
topicos.comparacao: English finds out who is the subject and who is the object by position: “the man sees the dog” and “the dog sees the man” are different because the order changes. The article “the” never changes.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: The accusative: the direct object changes only in the masculine
topicos.explicacao: German has four cases. For now you need two: the NOMINATIVE (who does the action) and the ACCUSATIVE (the direct object: what is eaten, drunk, bought or had). The only difference between the two is in the MASCULINE singular: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same. Verbs that take the accusative: essen, trinken, kaufen, haben, nehmen, möchten, lesen, sehen.
topicos.comparacao: English does not change the article: «the cheese» is the same as a subject or as an object (only pronouns change: «he» / «him»). German changes only the masculine: «der Käse» (subject) versus «den Käse» (object).

tabela.example: Ich esse den Käse. Ich trinke einen Saft.

topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Compare the sentences. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: Which gender changes form when it goes from subject to object? STEP 4: What happens to ein in the masculine? STEP 5: Who is the subject in Ich kaufe den Tisch? And the object?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: Verbs that change e to i or ie
topicos.explicacao: A group of very common verbs changes the vowel «e» to «i» or «ie» in the «du» and in the «er / sie / es»: essen → du isst, er isst. The other pronouns are regular. In «nehmen» the consonant also changes (nimmst, nimmt). Learn each of these verbs together with its «du» and its «er» form.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: Möchten e a moldura da frase
topicos.explicacao: «Ich möchte» is «I would like» or «I want» (more polite than «wollen»). The modal verb stays in 2nd position, and the other verb goes to the END, in the infinitive: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken.» This is the «frame» of the sentence. If the meaning is already clear, the second verb can be left out: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee.» To order: «Ich nehme …», «Ich möchte …», «Die Rechnung, bitte» and «Zahlen, bitte».
topicos.comparacao: In English «I would like to drink a coffee» keeps the verbs together. In German, the second verb goes to the end: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken».

erros.motivo: The second verb goes to the END of the sentence.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is forgetting the -en of the masculine in the direct object (Ich habe ein Hund instead of einen Hund) or using the accusative after the verb sein (Das ist einen Tisch instead of ein Tisch). topicos.aulaTitulo: My daily routine
topicos.titulo: Separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
topicos.explicacao: Many German verbs have a prefix that separates: «aufstehen» (to get up). In the present tense, the conjugated verb stays in 2nd position and the PREFIX goes to the END of the sentence: «Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.» In the infinitive, or with a modal verb, the verb stays whole: «Ich möchte um sieben Uhr aufstehen.» Common separable prefixes: auf-, an-, ein-, mit-, ab-, fern-, aus-, zurück-. Other prefixes do NOT separate: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-: «Ich besuche meine Oma» (besuchen).
topicos.comparacao: English has two-part verbs too («get up», «call up», «pick up»), but there the little word usually stays next to the verb. In German the prefix goes to the end of the sentence, and the sentence is «framed» between the verb and the prefix.

tabela.example: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

tabela.en: She watches TV in the evening.

tabela.example: Der Zug kommt um acht Uhr an.

erros.certo: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
erros.motivo: The separable prefix goes to the end of the sentence.

To say WHEN: «um» + hour (um sieben Uhr), «am» + part of the day (am Morgen, am Mittag, am Abend; but «in der Nacht»), «von … bis» (von neun bis siebzehn Uhr), «jeden Tag» and the adverbs «morgens, mittags, abends, nachts» (for what repeats).

STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Town and directions
topicos.titulo: Wo? e Wohin?: «in» and «to»
topicos.explicacao: With «in», German distinguishes WHERE you are (Wo?) from WHERE TO you are going (Wohin?). Wo? uses the DATIVE: masculine and neuter «im» (in dem), feminine «in der». Wohin? uses the ACCUSATIVE: masculine «in den», feminine «in die», neuter «ins» (in das). To go to a place there is also «zu» (always dative): zum (zu dem) Bahnhof, zur (zu der) Post; and «nach» for cities and countries: nach Berlin. The full cases come in lessons 11 to 13; for now, memorise the table.
topicos.comparacao: In English the preposition changes («in the park», «to the park» or «into the park»). In German the preposition is the same («in»), and it is the article that changes.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Town and directions
topicos.titulo: Asking for and giving directions (formal imperative)
topicos.explicacao: To ask: «Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post?» or «Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?». To answer, the formal imperative is used: the verb comes FIRST, followed by «Sie»: «Gehen Sie geradeaus.» «Biegen Sie links ab.» («abbiegen» is separable: the prefix goes to the end.) «Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße rechts.» Other useful expressions: an der Ampel (at the traffic light), an der Kreuzung (at the intersection), neben (next to), gegenüber (opposite), in der Nähe (nearby).

tabela.sentence: Gehen Sie geradeaus.
Biegen Sie links ab.
Biegen Sie rechts ab.
Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße links.
tabela.en: Take the second street on the left.

tabela.sentence: An der Ampel links.
Das ist nicht weit.
Es ist neben der Bank.
tabela.en: It is next to the bank.

topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: There is a second trap. English often uses “where” for two ideas (“Where are you?” and “Where are you going?”). German separates three: STEP 2: wo stationary, wohin with movement to there, woher with movement from there.
topicos.comparacao: In English, a yes/no question is built with «do» or by swapping the verb and the subject: “Do you live in Munich?” In German, there is no «do»: the verb simply goes to the first position: Wohnst du in München?

topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: nicht müssen = do not have to. Nicht dürfen = forbidden. Swapping them changes the meaning, just as «don't have to» and «must not» differ in English.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps.

tabela.english: I do not have to come.
I am not allowed to come (forbidden).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.titulo: Können: the first modal verb, step by step
topicos.explicacao: A MODAL verb helps another verb to say «can», «must», «want to», «may». Let's build the first one, «können». STEP 1: «können» says what you can or know how to do: «Ich kann schwimmen» = I can swim. STEP 2: conjugate «können»; it is irregular in the singular: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können. STEP 3: the second verb goes to the END of the sentence, in the infinitive: «Ich kann gut schwimmen.» The sentence is «framed»: the modal in 2nd position and the infinitive at the end. STEP 4: to ask a question, the modal goes to the front: «Kannst du schwimmen?» STEP 5: to negate, «nicht» comes before the verb at the end: «Ich kann nicht schwimmen.» RULE OF THUMB: «ich» and «er» are the SAME (kann) and never take -t.
topicos.comparacao: English also uses «can» + infinitive («I can swim»). The only difference is the position: in German the infinitive always goes to the END of the sentence; it does not stay next to the modal.

exemplos.ru: Kannst du Klavier spielen? — Ja, ein bisschen.
exemplos.pt: Can you play the piano? — Yes, a little.

erros.motivo: In the «er» form, the modal does not take -t.
The main verb stays at the END of the sentence.

topicos.explicacao: «Kannst du …?» (informal) and «Können Sie …?» (formal) are the most common way to ask for something. The main verb goes to the END, in the infinitive. Learn these classroom sentences: they work in any conversation with a German speaker and already appear in A1 exams. Remember that «langsamer» means «more slowly».

tabela.sentence: Wie bitte?
Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?

tabela.sentence: Ich verstehe das nicht.
Was bedeutet «Bahnhof»?

erros.motivo: The main verb goes to the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.titulo: Inviting with «möchten» and «können»
topicos.explicacao: To invite someone, use «Möchtest du …?» (informal) or «Möchten Sie …?» (formal), or «Kannst du …?» when it is a request («Kannst du um acht Uhr kommen?»). To ACCEPT: «Ja, gern!», «Gute Idee!», «Ja, das kann ich.» To DECLINE politely, say «leider» (unfortunately) and give the reason: «Nein, leider nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.» Always start with the word that answers: «Ja» or «Nein».

tabela.example: Möchtest du am Samstag ins Kino gehen?
Ja, gern! / Gute Idee! / Ja, das kann ich.
Nein, leider nicht. / Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht.
Ich habe keine Zeit. / Ich muss arbeiten.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is putting the infinitive right after the modal, as English does (Ich kann sprechen Deutsch instead of Ich kann Deutsch sprechen), putting -t on the 3rd person singular of the modal (er kannt instead of er kann) and swapping nicht müssen (do not have to) for nicht dürfen (forbidden). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.titulo: Müssen: obligation and necessity, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «müssen» expresses what you HAVE TO do (obligation or necessity): «Ich muss arbeiten» = I have to work. STEP 2: conjugate: ich muss, du musst, er muss, wir müssen, ihr müsst, sie müssen. The «ü» disappears in the singular and, as with «können», «ich» and «er» are the same, with no -t. STEP 3: the second verb goes to the END, in the infinitive: «Du musst pünktlich sein.» STEP 4: question: «Muss ich heute arbeiten?» STEP 5: with a separable verb, it stays WHOLE at the end: «Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.» In English we say «have to» or «must»; in German there is no verb «have» here: the modal does everything on its own.
topicos.comparacao: English says «have to» (the verb have + to) or «must». German has a verb of its own, «müssen», which is conjugated and leaves the other verb in the infinitive, at the end.

erros.motivo: In the «er» form, no -st and no -t.

erros.errado: Ich muss aufstehe um sieben Uhr.
erros.certo: Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.
erros.motivo: The whole infinitive goes to the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.titulo: Wollen: to want, and the difference from möchten
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «wollen» expresses a FIRM will or a plan: «Ich will nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren». STEP 2: conjugate: ich will, du willst, er will, wir wollen, ihr wollt, sie wollen. Careful: «ich» and «er» are «will», with no -t. And beware of a false friend: German «ich will» means «I want», not «I will». STEP 3: the infinitive goes to the end. STEP 4: «möchten» is more polite and softer («I would like»); «wollen» is direct («I want»). To ask a stranger for something, prefer «möchten»: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee», not «Ich will einen Kaffee», which sounds blunt.

linhas.example: Ich will heute Abend zu Hause bleiben.

erros.errado: Ich will einen Kaffee, bitte. (in a café, to a stranger)

erros.motivo: In the «er» form, the modal does not take -t.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.titulo: Dürfen: being allowed to (and the word «man»)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «dürfen» expresses PERMISSION: «Darf ich hier sitzen?» = may I sit here? STEP 2: conjugate: ich darf, du darfst, er darf, wir dürfen, ihr dürft, sie dürfen (the «ü» disappears in the singular). STEP 3: with «nicht», «dürfen» means FORBIDDEN: «Hier darf man nicht rauchen» = smoking is not allowed here. STEP 4: «man» is impersonal (like English «one» or «you»): «Hier darf man parken.» Careful: «man» has nothing to do with English «man» (that is «Mann»). It takes the verb in the «er» form. Signs use the infinitive or the noun: «Rauchen verboten», «Parken erlaubt», «Eingang», «Ausgang».

erros.motivo: The subject «man» is missing; it takes the form «darf».
Question: the modal comes first and «ich» takes «darf».

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is putting the infinitive right after the modal, as English does (Ich kann sprechen Deutsch instead of Ich kann Deutsch sprechen), putting -t on the 3rd person singular of the modal (er kannt instead of er kann) and swapping nicht müssen (do not have to) for nicht dürfen (forbidden). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the vowel changes only in du and er/sie/es. In ich, wir, ihr, sie the verb stays as in the infinitive.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: The imperative with «Sie» and with «wir», step by step
topicos.explicacao: The imperative is used to ask, give instructions, invite and command. We start with the POLITE form, which you hear in shops, schools and tests. STEP 1: take the infinitive («öffnen») and put «Sie» after it: «Öffnen Sie das Buch.» That is, the verb comes FIRST and «Sie» right behind it. STEP 2: separable verbs: the prefix goes to the END: «Hören Sie zu.», «Stehen Sie auf.» STEP 3: «bitte» makes the request polite and can go in several places: «Öffnen Sie bitte das Buch.» STEP 4: the «wir» form invites you to do something together (let's): «Gehen wir!», «Fangen wir an!» STEP 5: to negate, use «nicht» at the end: «Rauchen Sie nicht!»
topicos.comparacao: In English the imperative is just the bare verb («Open!», «Listen!»). In German the formal imperative looks like the infinitive, and what marks it is the ORDER: verb first, then «Sie» (English has no such word).

erros.motivo: In the imperative the verb comes BEFORE «Sie».
The separable prefix goes to the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the verbs. STEP 2: Now look at the commands. STEP 3: Questions: STEP 4: In which persons does the vowel change? And in which does it not change? STEP 5: Compare du sprichst and Sprich!. What happened to the -st? Does the vowel i remain? STEP 6: Compare du fährst and Fahr!. Does the ä remain? STEP 7: Where is the verb in sentences 5, 6 and 7?

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: The imperative with «du» and «ihr», step by step
topicos.explicacao: With friends, family and children you use «du» (one person) or «ihr» (several). STEP 1, «du»: take the «du» form of the present tense, drop the «du» and the «-st»: «du kommst» → «Komm!» STEP 2: if the verb changes e to i or ie in the present tense, the imperative KEEPS the change: «du nimmst» → «Nimm!», «du sprichst» → «Sprich!», «du liest» → «Lies!», «du gibst» → «Gib!», «du hilfst» → «Hilf!» STEP 3: if the verb has an umlaut (a → ä), the imperative does NOT have the umlaut: «du fährst» → «Fahr!» STEP 4: a stem in -t or -d gets -e: «Warte!» STEP 5, «ihr»: it is the same as the present tense without the «ihr»: «Kommt!», «Wartet!» STEP 6: «sein» is irregular: «Sei ruhig!» (du), «Seid ruhig!» (ihr), «Seien Sie ruhig!» (Sie). Separable verbs: «Steh auf!», «Steht auf!»

erros.motivo: In the informal imperative «du» is not used.
The imperative has no umlaut (a → ä only in the present tense).

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is conjugating du and er/sie/es without changing the vowel (du sprechst, er nehmt), changing the vowel in ich, wir, ihr (ich fähre, ihr sprecht → sprechet) or leaving the -st or -t in the du imperative (Gibst / Gibt mir! instead of Gib mir!). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: There is a second trap. English uses “not” (with “don't”) for everything: “I don't have a car. I don't live in Berlin.” German splits the job between two words, nicht and kein. And, like standard English, German does not double the negative: Ich habe nichts.Ich habe nie Zeit. Without nicht. STEP 2: is there an ein in the affirmative sentence? Replace it with kein. No ein? Use nicht.
topicos.comparacao: English has a single “not”, always tied to the verb (with “do”): “I do not live in Berlin. I do not have a car. I do not have time.” German divides the job between two words and does not put the negation in front of the verb.

tabela.english: I do not live in Berlin.
tabela.avoid: negates the verb or the place: nicht

tabela.english: I do not have a car.
tabela.avoid: negates a noun without an article or with ein: kein

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: The pronouns in the accusative, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the DIRECT OBJECT is what undergoes the action: in «Ich sehe den Mann», the one I see is «den Mann». STEP 2: so as not to repeat the word, we replace the object with a pronoun: «Ich sehe den Mann» → «Ich sehe ihn.» STEP 3: the pronoun follows the GENDER of the word replaced: «der Tisch» → «ihn»; «die Lampe» → «sie»; «das Buch» → «es»; «die Bücher» → «sie». STEP 4: for people, the pronouns for «I» and «you» change form: «ich» → «mich», «du» → «dich». STEP 5: watch out for «sie» (she, they) and «Sie» (you, formal): the context and the capital letter show which is which. Remember that only the masculine changes in the article (den); in the pronouns, all of them change: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns, ihr → euch.
topicos.comparacao: English also changes pronouns («I see him», «she sees me»), but uses «it» for every thing. In German each pronoun has its own accusative form, and for things the choice depends on the gender of the word: ihn, sie or es, where English has only «it».

exemplos.ru: Wo ist der Schlüssel? Ich suche ihn.
exemplos.pt: Where is the key? I am looking for it.

exemplos.ru: Wo ist die Tasche? Ich finde sie nicht.
exemplos.pt: Where is the bag? I cannot find it.

exemplos.ru: Das Buch ist gut. Ich lese es gern.
exemplos.pt: The book is good. I like reading it.

erros.motivo: The direct object requires the accusative.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Compare each pair. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: When does ein or nothing become kein? STEP 4: When does nicht appear? STEP 5: Where is the nicht when the sentence has no adjective or place?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: «Kein» and «keine»: negating a noun, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «kein» negates NOUNS. Use it in place of «ein» or when the noun has no article: «Ich habe ein Auto» → «Ich habe kein Auto.»; «Ich habe Zeit» → «Ich habe keine Zeit.» STEP 2: «kein» has the endings of «ein»: masculine: kein (nominative) and keinen (accusative); feminine: keine; neuter: kein; plural: keine. STEP 3: fixed expressions with «haben»: «Ich habe keinen Hunger», «keinen Durst», «keine Zeit», «keine Lust», «keine Ahnung» (no idea). STEP 4: remember that the masculine direct object gets -en: «keinen Hunger», «keinen Kaffee».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: «Nicht»: where to put it, and how to answer with «doch»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «kein» negates NOUNS; «nicht» negates EVERYTHING ELSE: the verb, the whole sentence, an adjective or an adverb. STEP 2: if it negates the whole sentence, «nicht» goes at the END: «Ich arbeite heute nicht.» STEP 3: if it negates an adjective or adverb, it goes BEFORE it: «Das Buch ist nicht teuer.» STEP 4: with a separable verb, «nicht» comes before the prefix: «Ich stehe nicht auf.» STEP 5: with modals, it comes before the infinitive: «Ich kann nicht kommen.» STEP 6: if someone asks in a NEGATIVE way («Hast du keine Zeit?»), the answer is «DOCH» to say «yes, I do» and «Nein» to say «no, I don't». «Doch» is the word that contradicts a negation. English has no single word for it.

tabela.example: Hast du keine Zeit? — Doch, ich habe Zeit!
Hast du keine Zeit? — Nein, ich habe keine Zeit.

erros.errado: Hast du keine Zeit? — Ja, ich habe Zeit.
erros.certo: Hast du keine Zeit? — Doch, ich habe Zeit.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is copying the English “not” and putting it next to the verb (Ich nicht wohne) or saying nicht ein instead of kein (Das ist nicht ein Tisch). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Shopping and clothes
topicos.titulo: Colours and the adjective after «sein»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to describe something with «sein», the adjective comes AFTER the verb and does NOT change: «Die Jacke ist blau», «Die Schuhe sind schwarz». No ending is added, just as in English («blue» for the jacket and for the shoes). STEP 2: ask «Welche Farbe hat …?» (which colour does … have?) or «Wie ist …?». STEP 3: colours are always written in lowercase here, because they are adjectives. STEP 4: the adjective can take «zu» (too): «Die Hose ist zu groß.» The change in the adjective ending (ein blaues Hemd) only comes in A2; for now, use the adjective ALONE, after «sein».
topicos.comparacao: In English the adjective never changes («the blue jacket», «the blue shoes»). In German too, after «sein» it is invariable: «ist blau», «sind blau». The difference only appears later, when the adjective goes before the noun.

erros.motivo: After «sein» the adjective does not change.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Shopping and clothes
topicos.titulo: Ask the price, read the amounts and say «too»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: for the price, ask «Was kostet …?» or «Wie viel kostet …?» with ONE thing; with several things, «Was kosten …?»: «Was kostet die Jacke?», «Was kosten die Schuhe?» STEP 2: read the amount like this: «25 €» = «fünfundzwanzig Euro»; «2,50 €» = «zwei Euro fünfzig»; «0,99 €» = «neunundneunzig Cent» (German writes a comma where English writes a decimal point). STEP 3: «zu» + adjective = too: «Die Hose ist zu groß.» STEP 4: the size: «Größe 38», «Größe M». STEP 5: three shop sentences: «Kann ich das anprobieren?», «Haben Sie das in Größe M?», «Ich nehme das.» STEP 6: «passen» takes the DATIVE of the person: «Die Jacke passt mir» = the jacket fits me; treat it as a ready-made phrase for now.

exemplos.ru: Was kostet die Jacke? — Sie kostet neunzig Euro.
exemplos.pt: How much does the jacket cost? — It costs ninety euros.

exemplos.ru: Was kosten die Schuhe? — Sie kosten achtzig Euro.
exemplos.pt: How much do the shoes cost? — They cost eighty euros.

exemplos.ru: Die Hose ist zu groß. Haben Sie sie in Größe 38?
exemplos.pt: The trousers are too big. Do you have them in size 38?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Shopping and clothes
topicos.titulo: Apontar: dieser, diese, dieses
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «dieser, diese, dieses» (this) follow the gender, like «der, die, das»: «dieser Pullover» (m), «diese Jacke» (f), «dieses Hemd» (n), «diese Schuhe» (plural: these). STEP 2: the masculine direct object changes, as you have already learned: «Ich nehme diesen Pullover» (accusative: dieser → diesen). Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same. STEP 3: use them to point at things in a shop: «Wie finden Sie diese Jacke?», «Ich nehme dieses Hemd.»

topicos.aulaTitulo: Jobs and the workplace
topicos.titulo: Saying your profession: no article, and the feminine in -in
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: with «sein» (and «werden»), the profession comes WITHOUT an article: «Ich bin Lehrer», and not «Ich bin ein Lehrer». STEP 2: the feminine form usually adds -in to the masculine: Lehrer → Lehrerin, Student → Studentin, Kellner → Kellnerin. STEP 3: some words get an umlaut: Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin. STEP 4: questions: «Was sind Sie von Beruf?» (formal), «Was bist du von Beruf?» (informal) or «Was machst du beruflich?». STEP 5: another way to say it: «Ich arbeite als Verkäufer» (I work as a salesperson), also without an article. Careful: «Krankenschwester» (nurse) has a different masculine: «Krankenpfleger».
topicos.comparacao: In English you say «I am a teacher», with «a». German does NOT use «ein» before a profession (unless there is an adjective with it). Only the feminine has its own form (-in).

tabela.example: Ich bin Lehrer. / Sie ist Lehrerin.
Er ist Student. / Sie ist Studentin.

erros.motivo: The profession takes no article after «sein».
For a woman, the form is «Ärztin».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Jobs and the workplace
topicos.titulo: Where you work, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask «Wo arbeitest du?» or «Wo arbeiten Sie?». STEP 2: to say the PLACE, use «in» and the forms you already know from lesson 9: «der» and «das» words: «im» (im Büro, im Krankenhaus, im Geschäft); «die» words: «in der» (in der Schule, in der Fabrik, in der Praxis). STEP 3: to say FOR WHOM or AT WHICH COMPANY, use «bei»: «Ich arbeite bei Siemens», «bei der Post», «bei der Bank». STEP 4: the hours: «Ich arbeite von acht bis siebzehn Uhr.» STEP 5: ask «Wie lange arbeitest du?» (how long per day) and «Wann arbeitest du?» (at what time). STEP 6: two common situations: «Ich bin arbeitslos» (I am unemployed) and «Ich habe frei / Urlaub» (I am off / on holiday). In A2 you will see why «im» and «in der»; for now, memorise the pairs.

tabela.question: Wo arbeitest du?
tabela.answer: Ich arbeite im Büro. / in der Schule. / in der Fabrik.
tabela.en: In the office. / At school. / In the factory.

tabela.question: Bei wem arbeitest du?
tabela.answer: Ich arbeite bei Siemens. / bei der Post.
tabela.en: At Siemens. / At the post office.

tabela.question: Arbeitest du gern?
tabela.answer: Ja, sehr gern. / Nein, nicht so gern.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Home and housing: es gibt
topicos.titulo: «Es gibt»: saying what exists, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «es gibt» means «there is» or «there are» (literally «it gives»): «Es gibt einen Balkon» = there is a balcony. STEP 2: «es gibt» is a FIXED expression (it does not change with the subject); what EXISTS goes into the ACCUSATIVE: in the masculine, «einen» or «keinen»: «Es gibt einen Garten», «Es gibt keinen Garten». Feminine, neuter and plural do not change: «Es gibt eine Küche», «Es gibt ein Bad», «Es gibt zwei Zimmer». STEP 3: to ask: «Gibt es einen Balkon?» STEP 4: the difference from «haben»: «haben» has an owner («Die Wohnung hat einen Balkon»); «es gibt» only says that something exists («In der Wohnung gibt es einen Balkon»). Both take the accusative.
topicos.comparacao: English uses «there is / there are» or «has» («it has a balcony»). German has «es gibt» (there is) and «haben» (to have), and both take the accusative, the case of the direct object.

tabela.example: Es gibt einen Balkon. / Es gibt keinen Garten.
tabela.en: There is a balcony. / There is no garden.
Is there a supermarket around here?

erros.motivo: What exists goes into the accusative: «Balkon» is masculine.
«es gibt» does not change, even in the plural.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Home and housing: es gibt
topicos.titulo: Describing a home, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «haben» says what the home has: «Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer.» STEP 2: ask «Wie viele Zimmer hat die Wohnung?» STEP 3: adjectives come after «sein» and do not change: «Die Küche ist klein und hell.» STEP 4: the size: «Die Wohnung hat sechzig Quadratmeter» (written 60 m²). STEP 5: the rent: «Die Miete kostet sechshundert Euro im Monat.» STEP 6: WHERE (Wo?) and WHERE TO (Wohin?), with the pairs from lesson 9: «im Wohnzimmer» / «ins Wohnzimmer»; «in der Küche» / «in die Küche»; «im Bad» / «ins Bad»; «im Garten» / «in den Garten». Careful: for the balcony, «auf» is used: «auf dem Balkon» / «auf den Balkon».

exemplos.ru: Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer und einen Balkon.
exemplos.pt: The apartment has three rooms and a balcony.

exemplos.ru: Die Küche ist klein, aber hell.
exemplos.pt: The kitchen is small, but bright.

exemplos.ru: Ich bin in der Küche. Ich gehe ins Bad.
exemplos.pt: I am in the kitchen. I am going to the bathroom.

erros.motivo: After «sein», the adjective does not change.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Home and housing: es gibt
topicos.titulo: Reading a rental ad
topicos.explicacao: Ads are short and use abbreviations. Learn the most common ones: «Zi.» or «-Zimmer-Wohnung» (rooms), «m²» (square metres, «Quadratmeter»), «€ / Monat» (euros per month), «NK» or «Nebenkosten» (extra costs), «ab sofort» (available now), «Balkon», «Bad», «Kü.» (kitchen). Example of an ad (original): «Schöne 2-Zimmer-Wohnung, 55 m², Küche, Bad, Balkon. Miete 600 € im Monat plus Nebenkosten. Ab sofort frei.» In English: «Nice 2-room apartment, 55 m², kitchen, bathroom, balcony. Rent 600 € a month plus extra costs. Available immediately.»

tabela.meaning: extra costs: water, electricity, waste collection, building maintenance

topicos.aulaTitulo: Free time, weather and hobbies
topicos.titulo: Gern, lieber, am liebsten: what I like and prefer
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «gern» (gladly) comes AFTER the verb and says that you like doing something: «Ich schwimme gern.» There is no verb «to like» here. STEP 2: «nicht gern» says that you do not like it: «Ich koche nicht gern.» STEP 3: «lieber» says what you PREFER: «Ich lese lieber.» STEP 4: «am liebsten» says what you like MOST: «Am liebsten tanze ich.» The order is: gern → lieber → am liebsten. STEP 5: useful questions: «Was machst du gern?», «Was machst du am Wochenende?», «Was ist dein Hobby?» STEP 6: «Mein Hobby ist Fußball» (one) or «Meine Hobbys sind Lesen und Tanzen» (several).
topicos.comparacao: In English we use «like» + verb («I like to swim»). German does not use a verb «to like» for this: the adverb «gern» goes along with the verb you do («schwimme gern»).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Free time, weather and hobbies
topicos.titulo: Talking about the weather: the impersonal «es», step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask «Wie ist das Wetter?» STEP 2: for rain and snow, German uses the verb with «es»: «Es regnet», «Es schneit». The «es» is required and does not replace any word (just like the English «it» in «it is raining»). STEP 3: with adjectives: «Es ist warm / kalt / heiß / kühl / windig / sonnig / bewölkt.» STEP 4: the temperature: «Es sind zwanzig Grad.» STEP 5: the seasons are «der» words and use «im»: «im Frühling», «im Sommer», «im Herbst», «im Winter»: «Im Sommer ist es heiß.» STEP 6: «Mir ist kalt» is a ready-made expression for «I am cold» (learned as a block).

tabela.sentence: Es regnet.
Es schneit.
Es ist sonnig und warm.
Es ist kalt und windig.
Es sind zwanzig Grad.
Im Winter ist es kalt.
Mir ist kalt.

erros.motivo: For a sensation, use «Mir ist kalt», not «ich bin».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Free time, weather and hobbies
topicos.titulo: Propor, concordar e combinar
topicos.explicacao: To suggest something: «Wollen wir …?» (shall we?), «Hast du Lust auf …?» (do you feel like …?). After «Lust auf» comes a noun in the accusative: «Hast du Lust auf Kino?», «Lust auf ein Picknick?». To agree: «Gute Idee!», «Einverstanden!» (agreed!). To suggest something else: «Dann …» (then …), «Oder …?» (or …?). With bad weather: «Bei Regen gehen wir ins Kino.»

tabela.example: Wollen wir wandern gehen? / Hast du Lust auf Kino?
Nein, leider nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
Dann gehen wir ins Kino. / Oder wollen wir Rad fahren?
Bei Regen bleiben wir zu Hause.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Travel and transport
topicos.titulo: How you travel: «mit» + meio de transporte
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say the MEANS, use «mit» + article: «mit dem Zug», «mit dem Bus», «mit dem Auto», «mit dem Fahrrad», «mit dem Flugzeug», «mit dem Taxi» (English says «by train», with no article). For «die» words: «mit der U-Bahn», «mit der Straßenbahn». Learn them as ready-made blocks (the reason for «dem» and «der» comes in A2). STEP 2: «on foot» is «zu Fuß», without an article. STEP 3: ask «Wie kommst du zur Arbeit?» or «Wie fährst du?» STEP 4: «fahren» changes a to ä in the «du» and the «er» (du fährst, er fährt); «fliegen» and «gehen» are regular in the present tense. STEP 5: the DESTINATION: «nach» with cities and countries («nach Berlin», «nach Brasilien»); «zu» with places and people («zum Bahnhof», «zur Schule»).

tabela.sentence: Ich fahre mit dem Zug.
Er fährt mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.

tabela.means: das Auto / das Fahrrad / das Taxi
tabela.sentence: Wir fahren mit dem Auto.
Sie fliegt mit dem Flugzeug nach Berlin.
Ich fahre mit der U-Bahn.
Ich gehe zu Fuß.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Travel and transport
topicos.titulo: Buying a ticket and reading the timetable, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask with «bitte»: «Eine Fahrkarte nach München, bitte.» STEP 2: the clerk asks «Einfach oder hin und zurück?» (single or return). STEP 3: ask the time: «Wann fährt der Zug nach München?» and answer with «abfahren» (separable): «Der Zug fährt um vierzehn Uhr fünfzehn ab.» Arrival: «Er kommt um sechzehn Uhr an.» STEP 4: transport timetables use the 24-hour clock, as in lesson 6. STEP 5: «Von Gleis 5» (from platform 5). STEP 6: duration: «Wie lange dauert die Fahrt?» — «Drei Stunden.» STEP 7: changing trains: «Sie müssen in Frankfurt umsteigen.» (separable).

tabela.sentence: Eine Fahrkarte nach München, bitte.
Einfach oder hin und zurück?
Wann fährt der Zug nach München?
Der Zug fährt um 14.15 Uhr ab.
Er fährt von Gleis 5.
Die Fahrt dauert drei Stunden.
Sie müssen in Frankfurt umsteigen.

erros.errado: Der Zug abfährt um acht Uhr.
erros.certo: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr ab.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Travel and transport
topicos.titulo: Booking a room, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask whether there is a vacancy: «Haben Sie ein Einzelzimmer frei?» or say: «Ich möchte ein Zimmer reservieren.» STEP 2: say for how many nights: «Für zwei Nächte» («Nacht» forms the plural «Nächte»). STEP 3: ask the price: «Was kostet das Zimmer pro Nacht?» STEP 4: ask about breakfast: «Ist das Frühstück dabei?» STEP 5: payment: «Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?» STEP 6: at check-out: «Ich möchte bitte bezahlen.»

tabela.sentence: Haben Sie ein Einzelzimmer frei?
Für zwei Nächte, bitte.
Was kostet das Zimmer pro Nacht?
Ist das Frühstück dabei?
Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?

topicos.aulaTitulo: A1 review and mock test
topicos.titulo: All of A1 in one table
topicos.explicacao: This table sums up lessons 1 to 19. Re-read one line at a time and say an example of your own out loud. If a line seems strange, go back to the lesson indicated or open the topic in the Grammar tab.
