topicos.aulaTitulo: A1 review and mock test
topicos.titulo: The 14 most common mistakes of A1
topicos.explicacao: Read each pair out loud: first the wrong one (to recognise the strange sound), then the right one. Correcting just these 14 makes your German much more natural.

erros.motivo: The second verb goes to the END.

erros.certo: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

erros.motivo: In the «er» form, the modal does not take -t.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: spoken past = auxiliary in position 2 + participle at the end. Movement or change = sein.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: The Perfekt, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the Perfekt is the past of CONVERSATION and messages: «Ich habe Deutsch gelernt» (I studied German / I have learned German). STEP 2: it has TWO elements: the auxiliary «haben», conjugated, in 2nd position, and the PARTIZIP II, at the END of the sentence (the frame you already know from modals). STEP 3: the Partizip II of regular verbs is «ge-» + stem + «-t» (like English «-ed»): machen → gemacht; lernen → gelernt; spielen → gespielt; kaufen → gekauft; kochen → gekocht; hören → gehört. STEP 4: conjugate «haben»: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben. STEP 5: yes/no question: «Hast du schon gegessen?» and answer: «Ja, schon» or «Nein, noch nicht». STEP 6: use the past time words: gestern, letzte Woche, letztes Jahr.
topicos.comparacao: English has two past forms: «I have done» (present perfect) and «I did» (simple past). The German Perfekt is built like «I have done», but in conversation it does the work of both: auxiliary + participle at the end.

erros.motivo: The Partizip II goes to the END of the sentence.
Regular verbs end in -t, not in -en.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the sentences. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: Where are haben and sein in the sentence? And the participle? STEP 4: Almost all participles begin with ge-. In which sentences is the ge- “hidden”? Where does it appear? STEP 5: In sentences 4 and 5, which verbs use sein? What do aufstehen and kommen have in common? Compare gekocht and getrunken. Which one ends in -t and which one ends in -en?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: Special cases of the regular Partizip II
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: if the stem ends in -t or -d, the participle gets «-et» so that it can be pronounced: arbeiten → gearbeitet; warten → gewartet. STEP 2: verbs in «-ieren» do NOT take «ge-»: studieren → studiert; telefonieren → telefoniert; reparieren → repariert. STEP 3: verbs with an INSEPARABLE prefix (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp-, zer-) also do NOT take «ge-»: besuchen → besucht; bezahlen → bezahlt; verkaufen → verkauft; erklären → erklärt. STEP 4: rule of thumb: if the verb begins with be-, er-, ver-, ent- or ge-, or ends in -ieren, it takes no «ge-» in the participle.

tabela.rule: stem in -t / -d
stem in -t / -d
-ieren: sem ge-
-ieren: sem ge-
be-: sem ge-
be-: sem ge-
ver-: sem ge-
er-: sem ge-

erros.motivo: The prefix be- already takes the place of «ge-».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: Regular separable verbs: the «ge-» goes in the middle
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the separable verb has prefix + stem: «einkaufen» = ein + kaufen. STEP 2: in the Partizip II, the «ge-» goes BETWEEN the prefix and the stem: ein + ge + kauft → «eingekauft»; auf + ge + räumt → «aufgeräumt»; ab + ge + holt → «abgeholt»; an + ge + meldet → «angemeldet» (stem in -d: +et). STEP 3: in the sentence, the whole participle goes to the end: «Ich habe heute eingekauft.» STEP 4: compare with the present tense: «Ich kaufe heute ein» (prefix at the end) × «Ich habe heute eingekauft» (participle at the end).

erros.motivo: The «ge-» goes in the middle, only once.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is using haben with verbs of movement or change of state (Ich habe gegangen / Er hat gefahren instead of Ich bin gegangen / Er ist gefahren; English «I have gone» tempts you to use haben), forgetting to send the participle to the end of the sentence or putting ge- in the wrong place in separable and inseparable verbs. STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 2: irregular participles
topicos.titulo: Strong participles of group 1, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: STRONG (irregular) verbs form the Partizip II with «ge-» + stem + «-EN» (and not «-t»). STEP 2: in GROUP 1, the vowel of the stem stays the SAME as in the infinitive: schlafen → geschlafen; laufen → gelaufen; fahren → gefahren; tragen → getragen; geben → gegeben; essen → gegessen; lesen → gelesen; sehen → gesehen; kommen → gekommen. STEP 3: there is no umlaut in the participle: «du fährst», but «gefahren». STEP 4: careful: «fahren», «laufen» and «kommen» use «sein» in the Perfekt (see lesson 23); for now, learn only the form of the participle. STEP 5: always learn the infinitive together with the participle: «sehen — gesehen». Memorising the pairs is the way.
topicos.comparacao: English also has irregular participles («done», «said», «seen»). In German the rule is: regular verbs in -t, strong verbs in -en (like English «eaten», «given», «driven»).

tabela.example: Er hat mir ein Buch gegeben.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 2: irregular participles
topicos.titulo: Strong participles of group 2: the vowel changes
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: in GROUP 2, the vowel of the stem CHANGES in the participle, which still ends in «-en». STEP 2: there are patterns that help: i → u (trinken → getrunken, finden → gefunden, singen → gesungen); ei → ie (schreiben → geschrieben, bleiben → geblieben); e → o (sprechen → gesprochen, helfen → geholfen, nehmen → genommen, treffen → getroffen, beginnen → begonnen). STEP 3: «beginnen» has an inseparable prefix (be-): no «ge-»: begonnen. STEP 4: there is no absolute rule: use the patterns as a help and memorise the pairs together with the infinitive. STEP 5: all of these use «haben», except «bleiben», which uses «sein».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 2: irregular participles
topicos.titulo: Verbos mistos e formas especiais
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: MIXED verbs have a different vowel (like the strong ones), but end in «-t» (like the regular ones): bringen → gebracht; denken → gedacht; wissen → gewusst; kennen → gekannt (like English «bring → brought», «think → thought»). STEP 2: «haben» makes «gehabt» and «sein» makes «gewesen»; «tun» makes «getan»; «werden» makes «geworden» (with «sein»). STEP 3: with «sein» and «haben», conversation uses the Präteritum more (war, hatte), but the participle appears in sentences like «Ich bin in Berlin gewesen». STEP 4: for «wissen» and «kennen», use «Ich habe das nicht gewusst» and «Ich habe ihn gekannt».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 2: irregular participles
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is using haben with verbs of movement or change of state (Ich habe gegangen / Er hat gefahren instead of Ich bin gegangen / Er ist gefahren; English «I have gone» tempts you to use haben), forgetting to send the participle to the end of the sentence or putting ge- in the wrong place in separable and inseparable verbs. STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 3: haben or sein?
topicos.titulo: Haben or sein? Step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: most verbs form the Perfekt with «haben». STEP 2: three groups form it with «SEIN»: (1) verbs of MOVEMENT from one place to another: gehen, fahren, kommen, fliegen, laufen, reisen, ankommen; (2) verbs of CHANGE of state: aufstehen, einschlafen, aufwachen, werden; (3) the verbs «sein» and «bleiben». STEP 3: rule of thumb: if you can say «from A to B» or «changed state», use «sein»; if not, «haben». STEP 4: the auxiliary «sein» is conjugated in the present tense: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind, ihr seid, sie sind. STEP 5: the sentence is still framed: «Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren.» «Er ist um sieben Uhr aufgestanden.» «Wir sind zu Hause geblieben.»
topicos.comparacao: English uses «have» for everything: «I have gone», «I have stayed». German splits it: «haben» for most verbs and «sein» for going, coming and changing.

tabela.sentence: Ich bin ins Kino gegangen.
Wir sind nach Berlin gefahren.
Er ist spät gekommen.
Sie ist nach Rom geflogen.
Ich bin um sechs Uhr aufgestanden.
Das Kind ist früh eingeschlafen.
Wir sind zu Hause geblieben.
Ich bin in Berlin gewesen.

erros.motivo: Movement from one place to another: «sein».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 3: haben or sein?
topicos.titulo: More verbs with sein and frequent confusions
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: more verbs of «change of state» that take «sein»: passieren → passiert («Was ist passiert?»); aufwachen → aufgewacht; sterben → gestorben; wachsen → gewachsen; werden → geworden. STEP 2: similar verbs that take «haben» because they change neither place nor state: verlieren → verloren; gewinnen → gewonnen; vergessen → vergessen. STEP 3: be careful with «fahren»: with a direct object it uses «haben»: «Ich habe das Auto gefahren» (I drove the car); without an object, from one place to another, «sein»: «Ich bin nach Berlin gefahren». STEP 4: the most common question: «Was ist passiert?» (What happened?). STEP 5: if in doubt, ask: «does it change place or state?»

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 3: haben or sein?
topicos.titulo: Question, negation and the words schon, noch nicht, noch nie
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the yes/no question begins with the auxiliary: «Hast du schon gegessen?», «Bist du nach Berlin gefahren?» STEP 2: the negation «nicht» comes BEFORE the Partizip II: «Ich habe nicht gearbeitet.» STEP 3: «schon» (already) and «noch nicht» (not yet): «Hast du schon gegessen? — Nein, noch nicht.» STEP 4: «schon einmal» (once before, ever) and «noch nie» (never): «Hast du schon einmal Sushi gegessen? — Nein, noch nie.» STEP 5: counting the times: einmal, zweimal, dreimal. STEP 6: with «sein», «haben» and the modals, conversation uses the Präteritum (lesson 24): «Ich war schon einmal in Berlin.»

tabela.example: Hast du schon gegessen? / Bist du schon gegangen?
Hast du schon einmal Sushi gegessen?

erros.certo: Ich habe noch nie Sushi gegessen.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 3: haben or sein?
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is using haben with verbs of movement or change of state (Ich habe gegangen / Er hat gefahren instead of Ich bin gegangen / Er ist gefahren; English «I have gone» tempts you to use haben), forgetting to send the participle to the end of the sentence or putting ge- in the wrong place in separable and inseparable verbs. STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Präteritum: war, hatte and the modals
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: war, hatte, konnte, musste, wollte, durfte work in speech. The other verbs in the past tense appear mostly in stories and texts.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps.

tabela.english: I had a lot of work.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Präteritum: war, hatte and the modals
topicos.titulo: Sein and haben in the Präteritum, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «Präteritum» is another form of the past, used more in WRITING and in texts. STEP 2: with «sein» and «haben», CONVERSATION also uses the Präteritum, instead of the Perfekt: we say «Ich war müde», not «Ich bin müde gewesen»; we say «Ich hatte Fieber», not «Ich habe Fieber gehabt». STEP 3: the forms of «sein»: ich war, du warst, er war, wir waren, ihr wart, sie waren. STEP 4: the forms of «haben»: ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie hatten. STEP 5: note that «ich» and «er» are the SAME (war, hatte), as with the modals in the present tense.
topicos.comparacao: English has the simple past: «I was tired», «I had a fever». In German, «war» and «hatte» do that job (and they even look like «was» and «had»).

exemplos.ru: Ich hatte Fieber und war krank.
exemplos.pt: I had a fever and was ill.

exemplos.ru: Als Kind hatte ich einen Hund.
exemplos.pt: As a child I had a dog.

erros.errado: Du warst krank? — Ich waren krank.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Präteritum: war, hatte and the modals
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the pairs. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: Compare ich war and er war, ich hatte and er hatte. What do you notice? STEP 4: In können → konnte and müssen → musste, what happens to the ä, ö, ü? STEP 5: In machte, wohnte, which suffix appears? And in ging? In sentence 5, where is zu?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Präteritum: war, hatte and the modals
topicos.titulo: Konnte, musste, wollte, durfte, sollte
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the modals also use the Präteritum in conversation: «Ich konnte nicht kommen», «Ich musste arbeiten». STEP 2: the form is: stem + «-te» + endings, and the UMLAUT DISAPPEARS: können → konnte; müssen → musste; dürfen → durfte; sollen → sollte; wollen → wollte. STEP 3: the endings: ich -te, du -test, er -te, wir -ten, ihr -tet, sie -ten (ich and er are the same). STEP 4: the second verb stays in the INFINITIVE, at the end: «Ich wollte kommen, aber ich musste arbeiten.» STEP 5: learn the contrast «muss nicht» × «darf nicht»: «Du musst nicht kommen» = you do not have to come; «Du darfst nicht kommen» = you must not come (it is forbidden).

exemplos.ru: Ich wollte kommen, aber ich musste arbeiten.
exemplos.pt: I wanted to come, but I had to work.

exemplos.ru: Als Kind durfte ich nicht lange fernsehen.
exemplos.pt: As a child I was not allowed to watch television for long.

exemplos.ru: Du musst nicht kommen. / Du darfst nicht kommen.
exemplos.pt: You do not have to come. / You must not come.

erros.errado: Ich könnte nicht kommen. (I mean: I was not able to)

erros.motivo: The second verb stays in the infinitive.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Präteritum: war, hatte and the modals
topicos.titulo: How to choose, and the forms you will read
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: in CONVERSATION, use the Perfekt for almost all verbs and the Präteritum for «sein», «haben» and the modals. STEP 2: in TEXTS (news, stories, books), almost all verbs appear in the Präteritum. In A2 you only need to RECOGNISE these forms, not produce them. STEP 3: the most common forms are strong and irregular (many look like English: kam = came, trank = drank, gab = gave, fand = found): gehen → ging; kommen → kam; sehen → sah; fahren → fuhr; essen → aß; trinken → trank; schreiben → schrieb; lesen → las; sprechen → sprach; nehmen → nahm; geben → gab; finden → fand. STEP 4: regular verbs make stem + «-te» (like English «-ed»): machen → machte; spielen → spielte; kaufen → kaufte.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Präteritum: war, hatte and the modals
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is putting -te on an irregular verb (gehte, kommte, sahte instead of ging, kam, sah), putting an ending on ich or er/sie/es in the Präteritum (er konnten / er gingt) or keeping the umlaut on the modals in the Präteritum (könnte/müsste have an umlaut in the Konjunktiv II, but in the real past they are konnte / musste without an umlaut!). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The four cases: nominative, accusative, dative and genitive
topicos.titulo: The four cases
topicos.explicacao: In German the function of a word in the sentence appears in the ARTICLE (and in some endings). There are four cases. NOMINATIVE: who does the action, the subject (wer? was?). AKKUSATIV: the direct object (wen? was?). DATIV: the indirect object, the one to whom something is given, said or helped (wem?). GENITIV: possession (wessen?). In «Der Mann gibt dem Kind einen Apfel»: «der Mann» is the subject (nominative), «dem Kind» is the one he gives to (dative) and «einen Apfel» is what he gives (accusative). You already use the nominative and the accusative; in this lesson the complete table begins.
topicos.comparacao: In English the function shows in the word order and in prepositions («give the apple to the boy»). In German it shows in the article: «dem Kind» already says «to the child».

tabela.question: wessen?
tabela.example: Das ist das Auto des Mannes.

erros.motivo: The masculine direct object goes into the accusative.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The four cases: nominative, accusative, dative and genitive
topicos.titulo: The complete table of articles
topicos.explicacao: This is the table that organises everything. Three shortcuts: (1) the FEMININE and the PLURAL hardly change; they only change in the dative and the genitive. (2) The NEUTER is the same as the nominative in the accusative, and the same as the masculine in the dative and the genitive. (3) In the accusative only the masculine changes. Other details: in the genitive, the masculine and neuter noun gets -s or -es («des Mannes», «des Kindes»); in the dative plural, the noun gets -n («den Kindern»), unless it already ends in -n or -s.

exemplos.ru: Der Mann gibt dem Kind einen Apfel.
exemplos.pt: The man gives an apple to the child.

exemplos.ru: Das ist das Auto des Lehrers.

tabelas.title: Indefinite article (ein, eine) and mein, dein, kein...

erros.motivo: Possession: genitive, and the noun gets -es.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The four cases: nominative, accusative, dative and genitive
topicos.titulo: Personal pronouns in the three cases
topicos.explicacao: Personal pronouns also change with the case. The dative is the one you will use the most, with verbs like «helfen», «gehören», «gefallen» and «geben». Order rule: the PRONOUN comes before the NOUN («Ich gebe ihm den Ball», «Ich gebe es dem Kind»). If both are pronouns, the accusative comes first: «Ich gebe ihn ihm».
topicos.comparacao: English also changes pronouns («I / me», «he / him»). German does the same and then extends the change to the articles.

erros.motivo: The pronoun comes before the noun.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The four cases: nominative, accusative, dative and genitive
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is forgetting the -en of the masculine in the direct object (Ich habe ein Hund instead of einen Hund) or using the accusative after the verb sein (Das ist einen Tisch instead of ein Tisch). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, antworten: all of them take the dative. Memorise the list as one block.
topicos.comparacao: The dative is the case of “to whom” and “for whom”. In English it appears in “I give it to him”, “give him”, “give me”. But there are three traps.

tabela.english: I give the book to the man.
tabela.ingles: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: The dative, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the DATIVE answers «wem?» (to whom?). It marks the person who RECEIVES, hears or benefits from the action, the INDIRECT OBJECT: «Ich gebe dem Kind einen Apfel»: what I give is «einen Apfel» (accusative, the direct object), and the one who receives it is «dem Kind» (dative). STEP 2: definite articles in the dative: masculine «dem», feminine «der», neuter «dem», plural «den». STEP 3: indefinite articles: masculine «einem», feminine «einer», neuter «einem»; the plural has no «ein» (with «kein»: «keinen»). STEP 4: in the PLURAL, the noun gets «-n»: «den Kindern», «den Freunden» (except those that already end in -n or -s: «den Eltern», «den Autos»). STEP 5: trick: masculine and neuter are the SAME in the dative (dem, einem); and the feminine «der» is the same as in the genitive. STEP 6: compare the three columns in the table and read aloud, column by column.
topicos.comparacao: In English the indirect object comes with «to» or through word order («I give the apple to the boy», «I give the boy the apple»). In German the preposition disappears and the article changes: «dem Kind».

exemplos.ru: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.
exemplos.pt: I give the book to the man.

exemplos.ru: Ich schicke der Frau einen Brief.
exemplos.pt: I send a letter to the woman.

exemplos.ru: Ich schenke dem Kind ein Spielzeug.
exemplos.pt: I give a toy to the child.

exemplos.ru: Ich zeige den Kindern das Foto.
exemplos.pt: I show the photo to the children.

erros.errado: Ich gebe den Mann das Buch.
erros.certo: Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch.
erros.motivo: The one who receives goes into the dative: «dem».

erros.errado: Ich zeige den Kinder das Foto.
erros.certo: Ich zeige den Kindern das Foto.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: Find out for yourself
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: Look at the indirect object. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: Which article becomes dem? Which ones? STEP 4: What happens to die (feminine)? And in the plural? STEP 5: What happens to the noun in the plural? STEP 6: Which object comes first: the dative (person) or the accusative (das Buch)?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: Pronouns in the dative, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: personal pronouns also have a dative form: mir (to me), dir (to you), ihm (to him, to it), ihr (to her), uns (to us), euch (to you all), ihnen (to them), Ihnen (to you, formal). STEP 2: they replace «dem Mann», «der Frau», «den Kindern» and avoid repetition: «Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch» → «Ich gebe ihm das Buch.» STEP 3: compare the three columns of the table: nominative («ich»), accusative («mich») and dative («mir»): careful, «uns» and «euch» are the same in the accusative and the dative. STEP 4: these verbs usually take TWO objects (dative + accusative): geben, schenken, schicken, zeigen, erzählen, leihen, anbieten, empfehlen. STEP 5: «wünschen» is typical: «Ich wünsche dir einen schönen Tag.»

exemplos.pt: He shows the city to us.

exemplos.ru: Ich wünsche dir einen schönen Tag.
exemplos.pt: I wish you a good day.

erros.motivo: The one who receives takes the dative: «ihm».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: In 30 seconds
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: With two nouns, the person comes first (dative): Ich gebe dem Kind das Buch.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: Dative and accusative in the same sentence: word order, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: if the sentence has TWO NOUNS, the dative comes first: «Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball.» STEP 2: if one of them is a PRONOUN, the pronoun comes first: «Ich gebe ihm den Ball» (dative pronoun + accusative noun) and «Ich gebe ihn dem Kind» (accusative pronoun + dative noun). STEP 3: if BOTH are pronouns, the ACCUSATIVE comes first: «Ich gebe ihn ihm.» STEP 4: remember the dative plural with «-n»: «den Kindern».

tabela.example: Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball.

erros.errado: Ich gebe den Ball dem Kind.
erros.certo: Ich gebe dem Kind den Ball.
erros.motivo: With two nouns, the dative comes first.
The pronoun comes before the noun.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 1: articles and pronouns
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is using the accusative with verbs that require the dative in German (Ich helfe dich / Ich danke dich instead of Ich helfe dir / Ich danke dir; English «I help you» looks like a direct object) or reversing the logic of gefallen and gehören (Ich gehöre das Buch instead of Das Buch gehört mir). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 2: verbs that take the dative
topicos.titulo: Verbs that take the dative: the person goes into the dative, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: some German verbs take the DATIVE for the person, even when in English the object looks direct: «Ich helfe dir» (I help you), «Ich danke dir» (I thank you), «Das Buch gehört mir» (the book belongs to me). STEP 2: these verbs do NOT use the accusative for the person: saying «Ich helfe dich» is wrong. STEP 3: memorise the verb together with «wem?»: «helfen + dative», «danken + dative», «gehören + dative». STEP 4: «helfen» changes e to i in the «du» and the «er» (du hilfst, er hilft). STEP 5: «gratulieren» takes «zu» + dative for the reason: «Ich gratuliere dir zum Geburtstag.» STEP 6: «antworten» takes the dative for the person and «auf» + accusative for what is answered: «Er antwortet dem Chef auf die E-Mail.»
topicos.comparacao: In English we say «I help you» and «I thank you», where the person looks like a direct object. In German the rule is fixed: with «helfen», «danken» and «gehören», the person ALWAYS goes into the dative.

tabela.en: We congratulate you on your birthday.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 2: verbs that take the dative
topicos.titulo: Gefallen, schmecken, passen: the German way of «liking»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «gefallen» reverses the sentence: the one who likes goes into the DATIVE and the thing liked is the subject: «Das Kleid gefällt mir» (the dress pleases me = I like the dress). STEP 2: the verb agrees with the THING: «Die Schuhe gefallen mir» (plural). STEP 3: «schmecken» talks about taste: «Die Suppe schmeckt mir (gut).» STEP 4: «passen» is «to fit» and «to suit»: «Die Jacke passt mir», «Die Farbe passt dir gut.» STEP 5: «fehlen» (to be missing): «Mir fehlt Zeit.» STEP 6: «glauben», «folgen» and «zuhören» also take the dative for the person: «Ich glaube dir.» «Sie folgt ihm.» «Hör mir zu!» STEP 7: «wehtun» (to hurt): «Der Kopf tut mir weh.» Careful: «gefallen» changes a to ä in the «er» form (es gefällt).

erros.motivo: The one who likes goes into the dative.
The verb agrees with the THING that is liked.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 2: verbs that take the dative
topicos.titulo: «Mir ist kalt», «Wie geht es dir?»: sensations with the dative
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to talk about SENSATIONS, German puts the person in the dative and uses «sein» (or another verb) with an adjective: «Mir ist kalt» (I am cold), «Mir ist warm», «Mir ist schlecht» (I feel sick), «Mir ist langweilig» (I am bored). STEP 2: to ask: «Ist dir kalt?» STEP 3: «Wie geht es dir?» (how are you?) and «Mir geht es gut» (I am well) use the same pattern. STEP 4: with the formal «Sie»: «Wie geht es Ihnen?» STEP 5: «Es tut mir leid» (I am sorry): «Es tut mir leid, ich kann nicht kommen.»

tabela.sentence: Mir ist kalt.
Mir ist warm.
Mir ist schlecht.
Wie geht es dir?
Mir geht es gut. / Mir geht es nicht gut.
tabela.en: I am well. / I am not well.

tabela.sentence: Es tut mir leid.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 2: verbs that take the dative
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is using the accusative with verbs that require the dative in German (Ich helfe dich / Ich danke dich instead of Ich helfe dir / Ich danke dir; English «I help you» looks like a direct object) or reversing the logic of gefallen and gehören (Ich gehöre das Buch instead of Das Buch gehört mir). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 3: prepositions that take the dative
topicos.titulo: Aus, bei, mit: always dative, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: seven prepositions ALWAYS take the dative: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu. Learn them in a row, like a song. STEP 2: «aus» = from (origin) or made of: «Ich komme aus Brasilien», «aus dem Haus», «aus Holz». STEP 3: «bei» = at the home of, at the place of, near: «bei Anna», «beim Arzt» (bei dem), «bei der Arbeit». STEP 4: «mit» = with (company) and by means of (transport, instrument): «mit meiner Mutter», «mit dem Zug», «mit dem Bus». STEP 5: after them, the article ALWAYS goes into the dative: dem (m), der (f), dem (n), den+n (pl). STEP 6: contraction: bei dem = «beim».
topicos.comparacao: English uses «from», «at … 's place» and «with» without changing the word that follows. In German, after these prepositions, the article changes form (dem, der, den).

tabela.example: Ich komme aus dem Haus. / aus Brasilien.

tabela.meaning: at the home of, at the place of
tabela.example: Ich bin beim Arzt. Ich wohne bei meiner Oma.
Ich fahre mit dem Zug. Ich gehe mit meiner Freundin.

erros.motivo: «mit» takes the dative; «Bus» is masculine: dem.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 3: prepositions that take the dative
topicos.titulo: Nach, seit, von, zu: always dative, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «nach» has two uses: AFTER (time): «nach der Arbeit», «nach dem Essen»; and TO with cities and countries (no article): «nach Berlin», «nach Brasilien». STEP 2: «seit» says since when something has lasted and uses the PRESENT tense: «Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren in Berlin» (I have lived in Berlin for two years; English uses «have lived», German uses the present). In the dative plural, the noun gets -n («Jahren»). STEP 3: «von» = of, from (origin, possession, author): «ein Brief von meiner Mutter», «vom Chef» (von dem). STEP 4: «zu» = to, towards people and places: «zum Arzt» (zu dem), «zur Schule» (zu der), «zu meiner Oma». STEP 5: contractions: «zu dem» = «zum»; «zu der» = «zur»; «von dem» = «vom». STEP 6: «gegenüber» comes after the noun: «dem Bahnhof gegenüber» or «gegenüber dem Bahnhof».

exemplos.ru: Nach dem Essen trinke ich Kaffee.
exemplos.pt: After the meal I have coffee.

exemplos.ru: Ich arbeite seit einem Jahr bei Siemens.
exemplos.pt: I have been working at Siemens for a year.

exemplos.ru: Ich bekomme einen Brief von meiner Mutter.
exemplos.pt: I get a letter from my mother.

exemplos.ru: Ich gehe zur Post und dann zum Supermarkt.
exemplos.pt: I'm going to the post office and then to the supermarket.

tabela.example: Nach der Arbeit fahre ich nach Berlin.
Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier.
Das Geschenk ist von meinem Chef.
Ich gehe zum Arzt. / zur Schule.
Die Bank ist dem Bahnhof gegenüber.

erros.errado: Ich wohne seit drei Jahre hier.
erros.certo: Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier.

erros.errado: Ich bin seit drei Jahren hier gewesen.
erros.certo: Ich bin seit drei Jahren hier.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 3: prepositions that take the dative
topicos.titulo: The contractions: beim, vom, zum, zur
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: in speech and everyday writing, the preposition and the article merge: bei dem → beim; von dem → vom; zu dem → zum; zu der → zur. STEP 2: there is no contraction with «dem» after «mit» in ordinary speech (you say «mit dem»). STEP 3: use the contracted form whenever you meet one of these combinations, that is, with the article «dem» (masculine and neuter) or «der» (only with «zu»): «beim Arzt», «vom Bahnhof», «zum Supermarkt», «zur Schule».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Dative 3: prepositions that take the dative
topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The mistake that costs the most is using the accusative with verbs that require the dative in German (Ich helfe dich / Ich danke dich instead of Ich helfe dir / Ich danke dir; English «I help you» looks like a direct object) or reversing the logic of gefallen and gehören (Ich gehöre das Buch instead of Das Buch gehört mir). STEP 2: Re-read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative and prepositions of place: Wo? × Wohin?
topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German chooses by situation and requires a case after the preposition. STEP 2: English “to” becomes nach, zu, in or für in German, depending on the destination. And “I have been studying for three months” uses the present tense in German, never a past tense. STEP 3: a preposition never comes alone. It comes with a case. Learn the two together.
topicos.comparacao: English uses the same few small words, “in”, “to”, “at”, “from” and “with”, for many different jobs.

topicos.titulo: Durch, für, gegen, ohne, um: always accusative
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: five prepositions ALWAYS take the accusative: durch (through), für (for), gegen (against; around, at about), ohne (without) and um (around; at, for clock times). Learn them in a row: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um. STEP 2: remember that in the accusative only the masculine changes (den, einen, keinen). STEP 3: common contractions: durch das = durchs, für das = fürs, um das = ums. STEP 4: «gegen» also approximates times: «Wir kommen gegen acht Uhr» (at about eight).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative and prepositions of place: Wo? × Wohin?
topicos.titulo: The nine two-way prepositions: a regra de ouro
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: nine prepositions change case depending on the question: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen. STEP 2: GOLDEN RULE: if the question is WO? (where, WITHOUT movement), use the DATIVE; if it is WOHIN? (where to, WITH movement), use the ACCUSATIVE. STEP 3: in this session, the three most common: «in» (in, inside), «an» (at, on a vertical surface, next to), «auf» (on, on top of). STEP 4: contractions: in dem = im; an dem = am; in das = ins; an das = ans; auf das = aufs. STEP 5: the article changes between the two cases in every gender: masculine Wo? «dem», Wohin? «den»; feminine: Wo? «der», Wohin? «die»; neuter: Wo? «dem», Wohin? «das». STEP 6: careful: «Ich bin im Garten» (state) × «Ich gehe in den Garten» (movement).
topicos.comparacao: English uses different words to show movement («in the garden» × «into the garden»). German uses the SAME preposition («in») and lets the case show whether there is movement.

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the remaining six follow the same rule: hinter (behind), neben (next to), über (above, over), unter (under, below), vor (in front of), zwischen (between). STEP 2: «Wo?» takes the dative: «Die Tasche steht vor der Tür.» STEP 3: «Wohin?» takes the accusative: «Ich stelle die Tasche vor die Tür.» STEP 4: «zwischen» needs a plural or two items: «zwischen den Büchern» (Wo?), «zwischen die Bücher» (Wohin?).

topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The costliest mistake is ignoring the difference between standing still (wo? → dative) and movement (wohin? → accusative) after the 9 spatial prepositions, or mixing up nach, zu and in when saying “I'm going to”. STEP 2: Reread the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Verbs of position and the N-declension
topicos.titulo: Stehen vs. stellen and liegen vs. legen, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German has TWO verbs for each position: one says WHERE something IS (state, Wo?) and the other says that you PUT something somewhere (movement, Wohin?). STEP 2: stehen (to stand, be upright) × stellen (to stand something up, put upright). STEP 3: liegen (to lie, be lying flat) × legen (to lay, put flat). STEP 4: the STATE verb takes the DATIVE, the MOVEMENT verb takes the ACCUSATIVE: «Die Vase steht auf dem Tisch» × «Ich stelle die Vase auf den Tisch». STEP 5: the forms: stehen – stand – gestanden; stellen – stellte – gestellt; liegen – lag – gelegen; legen – legte – gelegt. STEP 6: tall things or things that stand upright (bottle, vase, lamp, chair) use stehen/stellen; flat or lying things (book, newspaper, key) use liegen/legen.
topicos.comparacao: English mostly says «is» and «put» for everything. (It does have lie/lay and sit/set, but many speakers mix them up.) German always asks first: is it standing or lying? And that chooses the pair of verbs.

tabela.example: Die Lampe steht neben dem Sofa. / Ich stelle die Lampe neben das Sofa.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. / Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Verbs of position and the N-declension
topicos.titulo: Sitzen vs. setzen and hängen, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the same pair of state and movement applies to «sitting»: sitzen (to sit, be seated, Wo?, dative) × setzen (to put or seat someone, Wohin?, accusative): «Das Kind sitzt auf dem Stuhl» × «Ich setze das Kind auf den Stuhl.» STEP 2: forms: sitzen – saß – gesessen; setzen – setzte – gesetzt. STEP 3: «hängen» has both functions: state («Die Jacke hängt an der Tür») and movement («Ich hänge die Jacke an die Tür»); in the state use it is a strong verb (hängen – hing – gehangen) and in the movement use it is weak (hängen – hängte – gehängt). STEP 4: summary: stehen/stellen (upright), liegen/legen (flat), sitzen/setzen (seated), hängen (hanging).

topicos.titulo: N-declension: the «weak» masculine nouns
topicos.explicacao: A group of masculine nouns gets -n or -en in ALL cases except the nominative singular: der Student → den Studenten → dem Studenten → des Studenten. They are generally masculine people and animals: der Junge, der Kunde, der Kollege, der Student, der Herr, der Mensch, der Nachbar, der Polizist, der Tourist, der Name, der Löwe. «Herr» gets -n (den Herrn); «Name» gets -n in the accusative and dative and -ns in the genitive (des Namens). English has nothing like this, and it does not apply to other masculine nouns.

topicos.titulo: The trap for English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: without an article, or without a sign of gender and case, the adjective takes over that job. With a sign, the adjective just rests on -e or -en.
topicos.comparacao: English puts the adjective before the noun and never changes it: “new table, new tables”. German also puts it before the noun, but it changes by gender, number and case, and it depends on which article comes before it.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 1: with the definite article (der große Mann)
topicos.titulo: The adjective before the noun, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: after «sein», the adjective does NOT change: «Der Mann ist groß». STEP 2: BEFORE the noun, it gets an ENDING: «der große Mann». STEP 3: after the definite article (der, die, das), there are only two endings: «-e» and «-en». STEP 4: in the NOMINATIVE singular, it is always «-e»: der große Mann, die kleine Frau, das neue Auto. In the plural, «-en»: die großen Kinder. STEP 5: in the ACCUSATIVE, only the MASCULINE changes: «den großen Mann» (-en); feminine and neuter stay «-e»: «die kleine Frau», «das neue Auto»; the plural stays «-en». STEP 6: the ending repeats the case that the article has already shown: the adjective only «reinforces» it when the article is not enough.
topicos.comparacao: English never changes the adjective («the tall man», «the tall women»). German changes it by gender, number and CASE, but after der/die/das there are only two endings: -e and -en.

erros.motivo: Before the noun, the adjective takes an ending.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 1: with the definite article (der große Mann)
topicos.titulo: Dative and genitive: the «-en» ending
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: in the DATIVE, after der, die, das, the ending is «-en» in ALL genders and in the plural: «dem großen Mann», «der kleinen Frau», «dem neuen Auto», «den großen Kindern». STEP 2: in the GENITIVE, the ending is also «-en»: «des großen Mannes», «der kleinen Frau», «des neuen Autos», «der großen Kinder». STEP 3: sum it up like this: there is «-e» in only five places (nominative singular in all three genders, and accusative feminine and neuter); everything else is «-en». STEP 4: use them after the dative prepositions and the two-way ones: «mit dem neuen Auto», «in der kleinen Küche».

topicos.titulo: The typical mistake of English speakers
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: The costliest mistake is forgetting to give the adjective its gender ending after ein/mein (Das ist ein schöne Zimmer instead of ein schönes Zimmer), forgetting the obligatory -en in the Masculine Accusative and throughout the Dative, or putting an ending on the adjective after sein (Der Tisch ist große). STEP 2: Reread the table and say each correct sentence out loud before looking at the reason.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 2: with ein, mein, kein (ein großer Mann)
topicos.titulo: Ein, mein, kein + adjective, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «ein», «eine», «mein», «kein»… do not show the case in THREE places: masculine nominative («ein»), neuter nominative («ein») and neuter accusative («ein»). In those places the ADJECTIVE takes over the job and shows the case: «ein großer Mann» (-er), «ein kleines Kind» (-es). STEP 2: in the other places, the article already shows the case, and the adjective takes «-e» or «-en» just as after «der»: «eine kleine Frau», «einen großen Mann». STEP 3: nominative: ein großer Mann (-er), eine kleine Frau (-e), ein neues Auto (-es), meine neuen Autos (-en). STEP 4: accusative: einen großen Mann (-en), eine kleine Frau (-e), ein neues Auto (-es), meine neuen Autos (-en). STEP 5: rule of thumb: «-er» and «-es» only appear when «ein» has no ending: masculine nominative and neuter nominative and accusative.
topicos.comparacao: English has nothing like this. The logic is simple: German wants the case to show up ONCE; if the article (ein) did not show it, the adjective does.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 2: with ein, mein, kein (ein großer Mann)
topicos.titulo: Dative and genitive after ein: «-en» e «-er»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: in the DATIVE, after «einem», «einer», «meinen», the adjective ending is «-en» in all genders: «mit einem alten Freund», «mit einer netten Frau», «mit meinen alten Freunden». STEP 2: in the GENITIVE: «eines alten Mannes», «einer netten Frau», «meiner alten Freunde» (the ending is also «-en»). STEP 3: remember the dative plural rule: the noun gets «-n» (meinen alten Freunden). STEP 4: combine with prepositions: «mit einem netten Nachbarn» (N-declension!).

erros.certo: Ich wohne mit einem alten Freund.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 2: with ein, mein, kein (ein großer Mann)
topicos.titulo: The endings side by side
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: compare the two families: after DER/DIE/DAS: -e in Nom. sg. and Akk. fem./neut.; -en in everything else. After EIN/MEIN/KEIN: the same, but with «-er» (Nom. masc.), «-e» (Nom. fem.), «-es» (Nom. and Akk. neut.). STEP 2: the trick: if the article ends in «-r», «-e» or «-s» (der, die, das), the adjective takes «-e/-en»; if the article has NO ending (ein), the adjective shows the case (-er, -es). STEP 3: do not memorise the endings in isolation: memorise the MODEL PHRASES («der große Mann», «ein großer Mann», «den großen Mann», «einen großen Mann», «dem großen Mann», «einem großen Mann»).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 3: without an article (kalter Kaffee, gute Freunde)
topicos.titulo: The adjective without an article, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: without an article (neither der nor ein), the ADJECTIVE has to show the case ALL BY ITSELF. STEP 2: it uses the endings of the definite article: «der» → -er, «die» → -e, «das» → -es, «die» (plural) → -e. STEP 3: nominative: kalter Kaffee (m), kalte Milch (f), kaltes Wasser (n), kalte Getränke (plural). STEP 4: accusative: only the masculine changes, as always: kalten Kaffee (-en); the rest is the same as the nominative. STEP 5: it appears without an article with UNCOUNTABLE nouns (Kaffee, Milch, Wasser, Brot, Obst), with PLURALS without an article (gute Freunde) and in orders and prices: «Ich möchte kalten Kaffee», «Wir haben frisches Brot».
topicos.comparacao: English says «cold coffee», «cold water», «good friends» without ever worrying about case. In German, with no article, the adjective carries the case with the endings of «der, die, das».

erros.motivo: With no article, the adjective carries the ending (-es).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 3: without an article (kalter Kaffee, gute Freunde)
topicos.titulo: Without an article in the dative, and after viele, wenige, einige
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: in the DATIVE, with no article, the endings are: -em (m), -er (f), -em (n), -en (plural): «mit kaltem Kaffee», «mit kalter Milch», «mit kaltem Wasser», «mit kalten Getränken». STEP 2: after «viele», «wenige», «einige», «mehrere», the adjective also takes the no-article ending: «viele neue Bücher», «einige gute Freunde». STEP 3: after «alle», the adjective takes «-en»: «alle neuen Bücher». STEP 4: use no article to talk about people or things in general: «Ich esse gern frisches Obst.»

topicos.aulaTitulo: Adjectives 3: without an article (kalter Kaffee, gute Freunde)
topicos.titulo: The three families in one table
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German wants the case to show up only ONCE: on the article or on the adjective. STEP 2: with DER/DIE/DAS (the article shows the case): the adjective takes «-e» or «-en». STEP 3: with EIN/MEIN/KEIN (the article does not show the case in the masculine nominative and in the neuter): the adjective takes «-er» and «-es» in those places and «-e/-en» in the rest. STEP 4: with NO article: the adjective shows the case with the endings of «der, die, das». STEP 5: memory trick: «If the article fails, the adjective takes over.»
